options.text: About 2.7 million plus one, because there is only one new argument
options.explanation: This counts distinct arguments, which is what memoisation would compute. Without a cache, fib(31) re-runs the whole fib(30) tree and the whole fib(29) tree as well.

options.text: About 5.4 million, because each call makes two calls
options.explanation: Doubling would be right if both children were as large as fib(30). The second child, fib(29), has a smaller tree, so the growth per step is less than 2.

options.text: About 4.4 million: roughly 1.6 times as many
options.explanation: Correct. fib(31) runs the fib(30) tree (about 2.7 million calls) plus the smaller fib(29) tree (about 1.7 million) plus itself. Each step multiplies the work by about the golden ratio, 1.6.

options.text: About 2.7 million, because the recursion depth only grows by one
options.explanation: Depth controls stack space, not the number of calls. The tree grows in width at every level, so the total grows much faster than the depth.

workedExample:
1. A call is itself plus all the calls its two children make: fib(31) = one call + the fib(30) tree + the fib(29) tree.
2. The fib(30) tree has about 2.7 million calls and the fib(29) tree about 1.7 million, so fib(31) makes about 4.4 million.
3. The ratio between consecutive call counts settles near 1.6, the golden ratio, because the call counts follow a Fibonacci-like pattern themselves.
4. Small check: fib(4) makes 9 calls and fib(5) makes 15 (one plus 9 plus 5), also about 1.6 times as many.

The arguments 0 to 31 are only 32 distinct subproblems; memoising them would make about 32 distinct computations instead of millions of calls.

options.text: Θ(n) time and Θ(n) peak memory
options.explanation: This counts only the n calls and n frames (n is the list length). It misses that `xs[1:]` copies the remaining list on every call.

options.text: Θ(n²) time but only Θ(n) peak memory
options.explanation: The time is right, but each frame keeps its own slice alive until it returns. At the deepest point all n slices exist at once.

options.text: Θ(n²) time and Θ(n²) peak memory
options.explanation: Correct. For a list of n items, slicing copies n − 1, then n − 2, and so on, which adds up to about n²/2 copies. All those slices are still held by waiting frames at the deepest point, so peak memory is quadratic too.

options.text: Θ(n log n) time and Θ(log n) peak memory
options.explanation: This function removes one element per call, so there are n + 1 nested calls at the deepest point. Only halving the list on each call could give logarithmic depth.

workedExample:
Here n is the length of the list, and Θ means "grows at exactly this rate, up to a constant factor".

1. There are n + 1 nested calls (one per element plus the empty-list base case).
2. Each call creates a fresh slice one element shorter than its own input: n − 1 references copied, then n − 2, and so on down to 0.
3. Those copies add up to about half of n squared, which dwarfs the n additions, so time is **Θ(n²)**.
4. Memory: when the deepest call runs, every earlier frame is still waiting to add `xs[0]`, and each holds a reference to its slice. The retained slices have lengths n − 1, n − 2, ... 1, again about n²/2 reference slots, so peak memory is **Θ(n²)**.
5. Fix: pass an index, `total(xs, i + 1)`, so each call does constant work and memory is O(n) frames. (And for n above about 1000 in Python, use a loop.)
